questions.q: What are the four standard artifacts this lesson says make up a defensible solution blueprint?
options: A budget sheet, a timeline, a risk register, and a staffing plan
A conceptual data model, an integration diagram, a security/sharing model, and a user/access model
A single comprehensive architecture diagram containing everything
A requirements document, a test plan, a deployment plan, and a training plan
questions.explain: These four artifacts each answer a distinct question (entities/relationships, systems/flow, who can see what, how each persona actually gets in) and cross-reference each other rather than duplicating one picture.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the blueprint artifacts need to cross-reference each other rather than stand as independent diagrams?
options: Because Salesforce requires all diagrams to be submitted as a single PDF file
Because cross-referencing is only needed for scenarios with more than three personas
Because independent diagrams take longer to draw than connected ones

Because a panel reading one artifact should still understand roughly what another artifact must contain, which is what makes four diagrams read as one coherent design instead of four disconnected ones
questions.explain: The cross-referencing is exactly what turns separate artifacts into one coherent blueprint rather than four unrelated pictures.

questions.q: What level of detail belongs in a conceptual data model, according to this lesson?
options: Every field on every object, including field types and validation rules
Only the Apex classes that will implement the data model
Core entities and how they relate to each other, deliberately leaving out field-level implementation detail
A full entity-relationship diagram including index definitions
questions.explain: Going too deep into field-level detail in a blueprint wastes time that belongs in a lower-level technical design or the security model, and signals the candidate hasn't distinguished blueprint-level from implementation-level detail.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an integration diagram needs to label the direction and triggering event of each flow, not just draw boxes and arrows?
options: Because a diagram without a labeled trigger or direction can't actually answer a question like "what happens if that sync fails halfway through," even though it looks complete
Because unlabeled diagrams are against Salesforce's official documentation standards
Because direction and trigger labels are only needed for real-time integrations, never batch ones
Because panels never ask questions about integration failure scenarios
questions.explain: A diagram that looks complete but omits the trigger or direction actually answers less than it appears to — a specific failure-mode question exposes that gap immediately.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend keeping the security/sharing model and the user/access model as two separate artifacts?
options: Because Salesforce technically cannot represent both in the same diagram
Because the user/access model is always more important and should replace the security model entirely
Because only the security/sharing model is required for a passing design
Because conflating "what the sharing rules say" with "what a specific persona actually experiences" answers two related but distinct questions a panel might ask separately
questions.explain: The two artifacts answer genuinely different questions — the underlying rule set versus a specific persona's actual experience — and conflating them is a common blueprint mistake this lesson warns against.
